title: Built a brutally honest futures backtester. Looking for beta testers
author: kawash125
selftext:
My live bot lost its first 3 trades in 2 days. The backtest was filling orders on the signal bar. Classic.

So I built Kapybar. Describe your strategy to Claude or ChatGPT (any language, voice, even a screenshot), confirm the rules, and it runs on 40 liquid CME futures (ES, NQ, CL, GC, ZN… + micros), 1-min to daily, back to 2008.

\- next-bar fills, real rolls, commissions

\- always vs buy-and-hold

\- flags luck and edges that die with one more tick of cost

\- last 2 years hidden until your final verdict (3 shots per market)

\- prop-firm pass odds, minus luck

It tests your ideas, it doesn't make them up. If something passes, it means something.

Looking for serious rule-based traders. Needs Claude or ChatGPT Plus (MCP connector, 2 min setup). Free during beta.

No money, no broker access, no API keys.

Comment how you trade and I'll send an invite.

Not financial advice.

comments.author: investigatormaker
comments.body:
Since Kapybar needs Claude or ChatGPT Plus for the MCP connector, I would move that requirement to the first lines of the post instead of near the end. People who already pay for one of those plans are the testers who can start in two minutes, and the rest won't fill your comments. A short sample report, showing one strategy whose edge disappears after one more tick of cost, would also show the honesty better than a feature list can.

I make ThreadFox. It lets your AI research, write and publish Reddit outreach through your Chrome, within a job you authorize. Kapybar's free plan names the Reddit communities whose rules allow a post about it, quoting each rule: https://threadfox.vip/p/ddvuq

So far, are more of your beta signups on Claude or on ChatGPT?

replies.author: kawash125
replies.body: Too early to tell, so far it's Claude. Good point on moving the requirement up, thanks

comments.author: Maleficent-Success-6
comments.body:
The hidden two-year holdout is probably the feature I'd be most interested in.

One question though: how do you prevent users from indirectly optimizing against it across multiple research sessions?

For example, someone could test three versions on Gold, exhaust their attempts, then make small changes and test similar strategies on another market. Even without seeing the underlying data, repeated pass/fail feedback can gradually influence the research process.

I'm building TIYlab, a non-custodial Bitcoin portfolio automation project, and this is something we've been dealing with in our own strategy research.

We keep an experiment ledger, including rejected configurations, and preserve a sealed holdout rather than repeatedly using it to select winners.

But even that doesn't establish a live edge. You still need genuinely new forward observations after the strategy is frozen.

I'm curious whether your three-attempt limit applies to individual markets or to the broader strategy family across all markets.

replies.author: kawash125
replies.body: Per market (ES and MES share one). You're right that it doesn't stop hopping across markets and since every holdout covers the same two years, that leaks too. A cross-market counter is on my list. And agreed: the holdout can only reject; forward data is what proves an edge

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Hiding the last two years and limiting it to three shots per market is the right way to keep users from tuning to the holdout. A few things I'd want to see documented: how rolls are adjusted (back-adjusted versus spliced), how slippage is modeled per market and per time of day, and how "pass odds, minus luck" is computed, since it's the claim people will lean on. A per-session breakdown and a split around scheduled-release mornings (CPI, FOMC, NFP) would show whether a strategy depends on a few event days, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for those tags.

replies.author: kawash125
replies.body:
Good questions:

\- Rolls: rolled on volume; indicators use a back-adjusted series (causal), P&L uses the contract actually held

\- Slippage: flat, 1 tick per market/stop fill by default (adjustable), not time-of-day aware yet. Every result is also re-run with one more tick

\- Pass odds minus luck: same bootstrap paths run on a zero-edge twin (same swings, drift removed). The gap is the edge, with a 95% CI

\- Event-day split (CPI/FOMC/NFP): not yet, good idea :)

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Thanks for the detailed answers. The zero-edge twin with a 95% CI is a clean way to define the luck adjustment, and re-running every result with one more tick shows how fragile it is. For the slippage, time-of-day awareness would matter most around the open and around scheduled releases, so that's worth adding when you get to the event split.
